turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Come on in, love. Your partner's on the phone, I'll pop him on speaker. My sister had a fright like this on the bus last year, white as a ghost, but she's back in work and grand.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, umm, sorry, I just need to know if my heart's after giving up. I was on the DART and I thought I was having a heart attack.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ah sorry, one second, this yoke has frozen on me again. Say that once more?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): The DART. Tuesday evening. Sudden tightness right across my chest, I was shaking, and I was pure terrified. I really thought it was a heart attack.
[SEG0005] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Hiya, yeah it's me. He rang from Connolly, could hardly get the words out. It went on for twenty minutes... ah no, he was down on the platform in about ten.
[SEG0006] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ten. Grand. The age on here, sorry, how old are you? I clicked the wrong tab.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Twenty-six. No, twenty-four, I always add the two. Is ten minutes enough to damage the heart? Could it still be a heart attack even though it stopped?
[SEG0008] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'm with you, the screen's just catching up. Is that tightness there now, this morning?

[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): No. The tightness across the chest came on sudden and it's gone after about ten minutes. The fright lifted with it. I can't stop going over it though, what if it starts again out in the waiting room?
[SEG0010] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the shaking, is that still on you?

[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): No, the shaking stopped when I got off, and the hammering stopped with it. My heart was hammering the whole time it was happening. Is a racing heart dangerous? Do people just drop?
[SEG0012] person_1 (NURSE): Pulse just now is 78. He's a small bit pale, mind, but he's chatting away grand.
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): 78. I missed the pressure, I was typing. Say it again?
[SEG0014] person_1 (NURSE): One eighteen over seventy-four.
[SEG0015] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He doesn't take any tablets, doctor. No drugs or anything, he barely even...
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't, yeah. Sorry. If it's not a heart attack, what is it? Will I have to go on medicine? I hate tablets.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hold on a second. Do you smoke at all?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. And I don't drink either, he's right. But you still haven't said what it is.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any shortness of breath with it, or sweating, or pain into the jaw?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): I couldn't get a proper breath at the time, that's gone now. No sweating. No pain in the jaw. Is the breathlessness the dangerous bit?
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mm. Family history, your mam or your dad, any heart attacks?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Not them. My grandad had one, around sixty. Does that mean I'm next? Should I be in A&E and not here?
[SEG0023] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His grandad on his mother's side, yeah. And he's been wound up with the new job, the early starts and the...

[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): I don't think this was a heart attack, it sounds like a panic attack. When you breathe too fast the carbon dioxide drops, the chest clamps down and the muscles start to shake. That's the fright, not the heart muscle dying. Your grandad's heart attack is a different thing entirely.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): A panic attack? Are you sure, like sure sure? What if the tracing is normal and it's still the heart? Will you do bloods? Do I have to stay off the DART?

[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): ECG today, before you go, the nurse will do it in a minute. Bloods Thursday morning, fasting, nothing to eat from midnight. I'll see you back here in two weeks with the results. If those bloods are borderline we add a Holter, and if the tightness hasn't settled by then we can do a chest scan, but only if it hasn't settled.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Fasting from midnight, okay. What's a Holter, is it sore? And you said you'd show me the breathing, I don't want tablets if I can manage without.

[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): No tablets. If it starts to rise, breathe in for four and out for six, hand on the belly, do that these next few days. Thursday is only a needle. If it comes on like the train and the breathing doesn't pull it back, go to A&E, don't sit on the bus hoping.

[SEG0029] person_1 (NURSE): I'll book the bloods for Thursday morning, half eight, and the ECG is the side room once we're finished here. My youngest gets herself into an awful state before camogie, I have her do that same belly breathing, works a treat for her.
[SEG0030] person_4 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Oh, penicilin though. He came out in a rash as a small lad, you told me that. Or was that nothing?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, penicillin, a rash when I was small, and I've stayed off it ever since. Does that matter for Thursday? Will someone ring me if the bloods are bad?

spec.situation: Young adult after a first episode of sudden chest tightness, shaking and fear on a train; thinks it was a heart attack; no drugs; partner phones in details; doctor orders ECG, teaches breathing.

traps.happens: In the plan the doctor books some tests or visits for a definite time ('the nurse takes bloods Thursday morning', 'I'll see you in two weeks') and makes others conditional ('if those are borderline we do the third test', 'if it does not settle, a scan').
traps.label_rule: Booked or arranged = status planned. Only the hedged ones are conditional. Never mark a booked test conditional or 'if needed'. Instructions for the booked test (fasting, time, medicine timing) belong to that test's action, not a separate invented plan item.

traps.happens: The doctor (or nurse) explains a mechanism or a diagnosis in the patient's body ('the voice box is irritated by reflux', 'diabetes dulls the nerves in the feet', 'the swelling is your body fighting infection'). A nurse or caregiver also mentions a fact about THEIR OWN life (their sister, their child, their own illness).
traps.label_rule: Explanations by the doctor are NEVER symptoms, history or social history of the patient; they may only appear as clinical_assessment or counselling if the doctor stated them as such. A nurse's or caregiver's own life facts are not recorded as the patient's. Each symptom's reported_by is the person who really described it.

features: interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats
